newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: MANDELA WILL CHALLENGE, NOT MUZZLE WHITE-RUN MEDIA.
newsitem.headline: MANDELA WILL CHALLENGE, NOT MUZZLE WHITE-RUN MEDIA.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela said on Tuesday that freedom of the press was not under threat in South Africa but promised "many years" of vigorous debate as long as the mass media remained in predominantly white hands.

"Media freedom is not, has not been, and will never be under threat in our country," Mandela said in a speech prepared for delivery at the annual dinner of the South Africa Foreign Correspondents Association in Johannesburg.

Freedom of expression in the media was not only protected by South Africa's new constitution and bill of rights but was prized by his ruling African National Congress (ANC), South Africa's first black head of state added.

"It is in the selfish interest of the ANC that we should have a probing, robust and critical media...a questioning media that seeks to expose the weaknesses of our inherited bureaucracy, security forces, judiciary and indeed the new politicians themselves who can easily be corrupted by power," Mandela said.

But, returning to a point he has made more than once recently, he said that "in terms of distribution of wealth and power, ownership, management and senior positions in the media are predominantly in white hands".

"We would not be talking about South Africa if this reality did not impact on the mind-sets of the actors in the media industry," the president said, according to a text of his speech made available in advance.
"Debate on all these issues will continue for many years...as the Fourth Estate transforms itself to become part of the new South Africa in both word and deed," Mandela added.

Mandela has crossed swords with the South African media on several occasions recently, alleging that some senior black newspaper journalists were doing the "dirty work" of their reactionary white bosses, by running down his government.

While acknowledging that South Africa's transition to mature democracy and a free economic market still has far to go, he has complained that not enough credit has been given for progress already made.
Some editorialists have warned Mandela that his attacks risk spreading a perception abroad that he would like a tame press.

He argues that in some specific cases, reports on internal wranglings and power struggles within the ruling ANC have overstepped the bounds of prudent speculation and violated the rules of acceptable journalism.
Mandela, 78, said public debate conducted in the media "should be within the normal bounds of decency".
"It should not be aimed without justification at impugning the integrity of any of the role-players," he added.
Mandela held a four-hour, closed-door meeting with a group of senior black journalists on Monday to thrash out differences on their handling of sensitive political news.
"We agreed to disagree, knowing that creative and healthy tension between government and the media is natural in a democracy," he said.
